newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian, Belarus leaders meet to mull integration.
newsitem.headline: Russian, Belarus leaders meet to mull integration.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Friday met visiting Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko for more talks on closer union between the two Slav states, both formerly part of the Soviet Union.
Yeltsin, who looked energetic and fit, welcomed the hardline Belarus president in his Kremlin residence, saying Moscow was committed to seeking closer ties with Minsk.
"Commonwealth with Belarus is the common desire of our peoples and we will not deviate from this path," said Yeltsin, kissing Lukashenko on the cheek.
Yeltsin and Lukashenko signed a pact in April 1996 forming a close economic community and opening the way for closer political ties.
But there has been little concrete progress in furthering integration since then, partly because of Yeltsin's long illnesses, from which he is only just emerging.
Yeltsin said in his state of the nation address to parliament on Thursday that reintegration with Belarus was a foreign policy priority but should not be artificially accelerated.
Moscow is seeking closer ties with Belarus at the same time as it wages a diplomatic offensive against NATO's plans to extend membership to Poland and other former communist states in eastern Europe.
Foreign diplomats say the talk of moving Russian borders westward is Yeltsin's strongest card in his strategy to thwart NATO expansion.
Last year's crisis in Minsk, which saw Russian mediators looking embarrassed and ineffectual as Lukashenko swept aside parliamentary opposition, did not help ties.

The Kremlin has said that in the first stage the legal systems of the two states should move closer together, norms on rights should be agreed, unified transport and energy systems created and borders and customs adjusted.
Lukashenko said on Wednesday he foresaw joint economic, transport, economic and military structures.
Among the difficulties Yeltsin hinted at on Thursday were the differences between Moscow and Minsk on economic reform. Belarus has moved slowly to alter its Soviet-era planned economy.
On Tuesday, Lukashenko's Prime Minister Sergei Ling said that despite integration with Russia being a top priority, Minsk would take its own path to the market economy.
Lukashenko ordered limits on political rallies on Thursday and banned his opponents from using post-independence national symbols, which he has scrapped in favour of old Soviet ones.
About 5,000 demonstrators protested against Lukashenko's pro-Russian policies last Sunday.
